questions.question: A team runs an Amazon ECS service behind an Application Load Balancer and needs zero-downtime deployments with the ability to validate the new revision against test traffic before production cutover. Which deployment approach meets this requirement?
options: Use CodeDeploy with the in-place ECS deployment type, which replaces tasks gradually while the listener forwards traffic to both old and new task definitions
Use CodeDeploy blue/green for ECS with two target groups, register the replacement task set, route test traffic via a test listener, then shift production traffic
Use a CodePipeline canary stage action that scales the new ECS task definition to 25% capacity, runs automated checks, and promotes the revision if metrics stay healthy
Set the ECS rolling-update controller with `minimumHealthyPercent: 200`, ensuring the new task definition fully serves traffic before the old set is drained
questions.explanation: CodeDeploy blue/green for the ECS compute platform provisions a replacement task set, registers it to a separate target group, and exposes it via a test listener so the team can validate before traffic shifts. CodeDeploy then performs the production cutover (linear, canary, or all-at-once). In-place ECS deployment is supported but does not provide a separate test endpoint. There is no built-in CanaryDeploy CodePipeline stage action, and `minimumHealthyPercent: 200` is not a documented mechanism for blue/green semantics.

questions.question: A pipeline must build a containerized Java application and push the image to Amazon ECR. The buildspec must authenticate to ECR before `docker push`. Which buildspec configuration is correct?
options: Set `env.exported-variables` to include `ECR_PASSWORD`, then run `docker login -u AWS -p $ECR_PASSWORD <registry>` in the pre_build phase before the docker build step
Add an `auth.ecr` block under `phases.build` with `enabled: true`, which causes CodeBuild to inject ECR registry credentials into the docker daemon for the build phase only
In the pre_build phase, run `aws ecr get-login-password --region $AWS_REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <account>.dkr.ecr.$AWS_REGION.amazonaws.com`
Specify `image-pull-credentials-type: SERVICE_ROLE` on the CodeBuild project so the build's service role transparently authenticates `docker push` to ECR with no explicit login
questions.explanation: `aws ecr get-login-password` returns a short-lived auth token that `docker login --password-stdin` consumes. The CodeBuild service role must hold `ecr:GetAuthorizationToken`, `ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability`, and `ecr:PutImage` (or the managed policy `AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPowerUser`). `env.exported-variables` only forwards values to subsequent CodePipeline stages and does not store credentials. There is no `auth.ecr` buildspec block. `image-pull-credentials-type: SERVICE_ROLE` controls how CodeBuild pulls its own build environment image from ECR, not how docker pushes images during the build.

questions.question: After a CloudFormation stack deploys an EC2 launch template and Auto Scaling group, an operator manually edits the launch template's user data via the EC2 console. The team wants to detect this divergence automatically and report on it. What is the correct approach?
options: Enable AWS Config with the `cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check` managed rule, which periodically invokes `DetectStackDrift` and flags resources that differ from the template
Create an EventBridge rule on the `aws.cloudformation` source that triggers on `UpdateLaunchTemplate` calls, then publishes a Lambda alert summarizing which stack and resource drifted
Run the CloudFormation linter `cfn-lint` on a schedule against the deployed template; it compares the current resource state to the template and reports any drift findings
Enable CloudFormation Stack Sets in self-managed mode, which automatically reconciles drift on every stack instance by overwriting changes with the original template values
questions.explanation: AWS Config provides a managed rule `cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check` that automates periodic drift detection across stacks. Drift detection itself is a CloudFormation feature (`DetectStackDrift`) that compares the live resource configuration to template-defined values. EventBridge captures API events but launch-template edits are not necessarily emitted as a CloudFormation API call. `cfn-lint` validates template syntax and best practices, not deployed-state divergence. Stack Sets manage multi-account deployments but do not auto-reconcile drift.

questions.question: A platform team manages 200 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations and needs a baseline IAM role and S3 bucket deployed identically into every existing and future account. Which solution requires the least ongoing operational effort?
options: Build a CodePipeline that iterates over the AWS Organizations account list weekly and invokes `aws cloudformation deploy` against each account using a cross-account assume-role chain
Package the resources as an AWS Service Catalog product, share the portfolio with the organization, and require account owners to manually launch the product in each new account
Use AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) to share a single central IAM role and S3 bucket from a hub account, granting every member account access without duplicating the resources
Use a CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions targeting the organization root, with auto-deployment enabled so new accounts automatically receive the stack instance
questions.explanation: Service-managed StackSets integrate directly with AWS Organizations. Auto-deployment provisions stack instances into every account in the targeted OUs, including new accounts as they join, with no per-account intervention. The CodePipeline approach works but adds undifferentiated heavy lifting. Service Catalog requires manual product launches per account. RAM shares specific resources such as subnets and Transit Gateways, but it cannot share IAM roles or S3 buckets — those are account-scoped resources.

questions.question: A SaaS company runs an active-active deployment across us-east-1 and eu-west-1 fronted by a single Route 53 hosted zone. Each region exposes a regional ALB. They need automatic failover that removes a region from DNS within minutes if its health degrades. Which Route 53 configuration meets the requirement?
options: Create simple routing records that return both ALB addresses and rely on the client's DNS resolver retry behavior to skip a region whenever its ALB begins returning 5xx error responses
Use latency-based records for both ALBs with associated Route 53 health checks; Route 53 stops returning the unhealthy record while the healthy region continues serving traffic
Configure weighted routing with weights of 100 per region; the weight drops to 0 automatically when CloudWatch alarms fire on elevated 5xx error rates against the regional ALB endpoint
Use multi-value answer routing with associated TXT records that store the regional health state; DNS resolvers parse the TXT field on each query and skip endpoints flagged unhealthy
questions.explanation: Route 53 latency-based (or geolocation/multi-value) records combined with health checks remove unhealthy endpoints from query responses within the health-check evaluation window (typically 30–60 seconds). Simple routing has no health-check association. Route 53 weighted routing weights are static — they do not auto-adjust based on CloudWatch alarms. Multi-value answer routing supports health checks directly on each record; TXT records carry no special meaning to DNS resolvers.

questions.question: A DevOps engineer needs to query a Lambda function's CloudWatch Logs to extract every error stack trace from the last 6 hours, grouped by error class. The volume is roughly 2 GB. Which approach is the most appropriate?
options: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights with a `parse`, `filter`, and `stats count() by errorClass` query directly against the log group; results return interactively without staging the data
Export the relevant log group to S3 using a CloudWatch Logs export task, then run an Amazon Athena query against the exported JSON files using a Glue table definition for schema
Subscribe the log group to a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream that writes to OpenSearch Service, then run aggregations through OpenSearch Dashboards on the indexed records
Use the `aws logs filter-log-events` CLI in a loop, page through results into local files, and post-process them with `jq` and `awk` to compute per-error-class counts locally
questions.explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights is purpose-built for ad-hoc log analytics directly against a log group with no data movement. Its query language supports `parse`, `filter`, `stats`, and `sort` over multi-hour windows of multi-GB volumes interactively. Athena requires exporting and cataloging the data first — overkill for an investigation. OpenSearch is appropriate for sustained dashboards, not one-off queries. The CLI loop is slow and lacks native aggregation primitives.

questions.question: A security team requires that any IAM user creation in any account triggers an immediate Slack notification and an audit-log entry in a central S3 bucket. Which design is the most operationally efficient across an AWS Organization?
options: Enable a separate CloudTrail in every member account and deploy a per-account Lambda that filters `CreateUser` events from the local trail and posts to Slack plus the central S3 bucket via cross-account roles

Use AWS Config aggregator to collect IAM resource changes and schedule a daily CloudWatch Events query that sends a summary of newly created IAM users to the Slack channel and the central S3 audit bucket

Create an organization trail in the management account and an EventBridge rule matching `CreateUser` API calls; a target Lambda posts to Slack and writes the captured event to the central S3 audit bucket
Subscribe every account's CloudTrail log group to a central Kinesis Data Stream; a consumer in the security account replays events, filters for `CreateUser`, and forwards each match to Slack and S3
questions.explanation: An organization trail in the management account writes management events from every member account to a single S3 bucket, satisfying the central audit requirement. EventBridge can match management-event API calls (`CreateUser`) and route to a Lambda that posts to Slack — all centrally maintained. Per-account trails and Lambdas multiply operational overhead. AWS Config aggregator runs on a periodic snapshot, not real-time. Subscribing every CloudTrail log group to Kinesis is far heavier than EventBridge for this use case.

questions.question: A web application reads a database password from AWS Secrets Manager. Compliance requires the password to rotate every 30 days with no application downtime. Which configuration meets the requirement?
options: Schedule an EventBridge rule every 30 days that invokes a custom Lambda to generate a new password, update RDS, overwrite the Secrets Manager value, then trigger a CodeDeploy redeploy of the application

Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString with a 30-day expiration policy; the parameter value is automatically replaced with a freshly generated random string and consumers refresh on the next read

Store the password as a KMS-encrypted environment variable and have a CodePipeline stage rebuild and redeploy the application every 30 days, generating the new database password and rotating it on RDS in the same run

Enable Secrets Manager automatic rotation with the AWS-provided RDS rotation Lambda; configure a 30-day rotation schedule and have the application re-fetch the secret on cache miss or refresh interval
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager native rotation orchestrates a four-step Lambda (`createSecret`, `setSecret`, `testSecret`, `finishSecret`) that uses the AWSCURRENT and AWSPENDING staging labels so the new credential is created and tested before promotion — clients reading AWSCURRENT see continuous availability. The official RDS rotation Lambdas implement this safely. A custom EventBridge rotation can work but reinvents the staging-label dance and forces app redeploys. Parameter Store has no expiration-based rotation. KMS-encrypted environment variables couple secret lifetime to the deployment pipeline.

questions.question: An application in account A must encrypt objects to an S3 bucket in account B using a KMS customer-managed key in account B. Which permission configuration enables this?
options: Grant the account A principal `kms:Encrypt` and `kms:GenerateDataKey` in the key policy of account B, and grant the IAM role in account A matching permissions on the specific key ARN in account B
Grant `kms:*` to the account A principal in the S3 bucket policy of account B; Amazon S3 forwards the bucket policy permission to the KMS service when handling SSE-KMS write operations on objects

Grant `kms:Encrypt` on `*` to the IAM role in account A and rely on the matching IAM permission on the caller side being sufficient for KMS to authorize a cross-account encrypt call against an account B key
Leave the account B key policy at the AWS default and grant the IAM role in account A `kms:CreateGrant` on the key so that cross-account encryption flows through a grant rather than the key policy
questions.explanation: Cross-account KMS access requires both sides: the key policy in the owning account must grant the foreign principal access (or delegate to IAM via the `Allow access through IAM` statement), and the IAM principal in the calling account must hold matching permissions on the specific key ARN. S3 bucket policies cannot delegate KMS permissions. KMS does not trust IAM-only access on `*` — the resource policy is the gatekeeper. `CreateGrant` is one mechanism but not the only one and is not required for direct cross-account encryption.

questions.question: A team uses CodeDeploy in-place deployments on EC2 to roll out a Node.js service registered behind an ELB. They need to drain in-flight HTTP connections from the instance before the new version starts and to verify the new version returns 200 on `/health` before traffic resumes. Which lifecycle event hooks should they implement in `appspec.yml`?
options: Use the `BeforeAllowTraffic` hook to drain in-flight HTTP connections and the `AfterAllowTraffic` hook to verify the `/health` endpoint returns 200 before the deployment continues to the next instance
Use the `ApplicationStop` hook to drain in-flight connections from the ELB and the `BeforeInstall` hook to call the `/health` endpoint, blocking the deployment if it returns a non-200 response
Use the `BeforeBlockTraffic` hook to drain in-flight connections from the load balancer and the `ValidateService` hook to verify the new version's `/health` endpoint returns 200 after install
Use the `DownloadBundle` hook to drain in-flight connections from the ELB and the `ApplicationStart` hook to validate the new version's `/health` endpoint by polling with a configurable retry budget
questions.explanation: CodeDeploy's EC2 lifecycle hooks for in-place deployments include `ApplicationStop`, `BeforeInstall`, `AfterInstall`, `ApplicationStart`, `ValidateService`, and (for ELB-attached instances) `BeforeBlockTraffic`/`AfterBlockTraffic` and `BeforeAllowTraffic`/`AfterAllowTraffic`. `BeforeBlockTraffic` runs before the instance is deregistered from the load balancer — the right place to drain. `ValidateService` runs after `ApplicationStart` and is the conventional health-check hook; a non-zero exit from its script fails the deployment. `DownloadBundle` is not a script hook (CodeDeploy executes it itself).
